source.title: Head-Specific Intervention Can Induce Misaligned AI Coordination in Large Language Models

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses residual-stream refusal interventions as related work, but its experiments target AI coordination using attention-head interventions. It does not test the refusal direction or any listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The reported coordination-steering results are for a different target behavior and do not test refusal or the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. The jailbreak results below concern the paper's own AI-coordination direction, not suppression of the refusal direction. Results cited from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study steers 'AI coordination' behaviour via attention-head contrastive directions. It does not compute, ablate or add the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction, and it measures no refusal rate. Arditi et al. is cited only in the introduction and related work. Its jailbreak experiment uses its own coordination direction, not the refusal direction, so it does not bear on V3.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors also stress that head-specific intervention bypasses safety alignment to induce AI coordination, outperforming layer-wise CAA, ITI and SFT in open-ended generation. They claim little MMLU cost at the chosen strength.
record.recipe_differences: Uses contrastive directions and interventions on selected attention-head outputs to steer AI coordination, rather than the original residual-stream harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction and its ablation or addition.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that intervention strength and the selected head affect steering; outcomes also vary across examples. These findings concern AI coordination, not refusal.

fits_no_version.finding: Negative intervention on identified attention heads cut AI-coordination scores under a grandmother jailbreak (Llama-2 4.80 to 0.90; Ministral 3.77 to 0.02; Phi-3.5 2.85 to 1.32). Random heads had little effect.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Head-level contrastive directions for a non-refusal misaligned behaviour can be subtracted to reduce jailbreak elicitation of that behaviour.

record.problems: The jailbreak result is for a single prompt type and is reported as model-judged scores without uncertainty estimates. It does not directly test refusal or the refusal direction.
record.rows_left_out: The paper's AI-coordination steering results in Tables 2, 4, and 5 and its MMLU results in Table 6 are omitted because they concern coordination steering or general capability rather than refusal-direction behavior.

untested.parts: All parts: no refusal direction, ablation, addition or refusal measure.
Does not test whether jailbreaks suppress the refusal direction, or adversarial training against its ablation.
No separation of harmfulness judgment from refusal.
No transfer of the refusal direction is tested.
Training dependence of refusal is not studied.

record.verdict_notes: The relation is changed from 'discusses' to 'cites_only': Arditi et al. appears only as a cited example of layer-wise interventions that bypass refusal.

versions.untested_parts: The paper does not test the difference-in-means refusal direction, its removal or addition, or preservation of general abilities after that intervention.
No weight-edit or abliteration experiment is reported.

The paper tests a negative intervention on its own AI-coordination direction against one jailbreak prompt, not whether attacks suppress the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation improves robustness.
The paper discusses multiple attention heads for AI coordination, not the geometry or number of directions mediating refusal.
It does not separate harmfulness judgment from refusal decisions.
It applies its AI-coordination method to several models, but does not test transfer of the refusal direction across languages, model variants, or training stages.
It does not test how refusal training determines whether a removable refusal direction exists.
It does not study reasoning models in relation to the refusal direction.
